extracted.intended_audience: BBC journalists, producers, editors and independent production companies working on BBC content (news, current affairs, factual programmes and online output)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial rules and standards for achieving due accuracy in BBC output, covering how to gather, verify, label and correct material across live output, online content, user-generated material, AI use, reconstructions, drama, archive and cross-nation reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy as weighing facts and opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is not simply a matter of getting facts right. Relevant opinions as well as facts may need to be weighed and considered to get at the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, content makers should gather material using first-hand sources; check facts and statistics and identify caveats; validate authenticity of documentary and digital material; corroborate claims and allegations; weigh, interpret and contextualise claims (including statistical claims). See guidance on Reporting Statistics and Investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due accuracy prioritised over speed
rubrics_metrics.description: In news and current affairs content, achieving due accuracy is more important than speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and producers should not sacrifice necessary verification or context for the sake of being first; apply extra caution to controversial issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer first-hand sources and eyewitnessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Content producers should try to witness events and gather information first hand. Where this is not possible, talk to first-hand sources and, where practicable, corroborate evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See specific guidance 3.4.20–3.4.23 on sources and corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reluctance to rely on a single source
rubrics_metrics.description: Content producers should be reluctant to rely on a single source. If they do rely on a single source, it should be credible, and a named, on-the-record source is always preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on a single source, assess credibility carefully and seek corroboration where practicable; see 3.4.20–3.4.23.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record research interviews when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Research interviews with sources making serious allegations should, wherever practicable, be recorded. If recording might inhibit the source, full notes should be made, preferably contemporaneously or as soon as possible afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Section 7 Privacy and 3.4.15 on note-taking; recorded interviews support verification and legal protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and verify information; disclose inability to verify
rubrics_metrics.description: Information, facts, documents and digital material must be checked and verified to achieve due accuracy. If content producers have been unable to verify material, they should usually say so and attribute the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear to audiences when information is unverified and attribute the source; apply extra scrutiny to documentary and digital evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in live content
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieving due accuracy in live content can be challenging as there may be little opportunity to verify factual claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify risks in advance, prepare sufficiently so content contains challenge or context, ensure contributors can provide challenge; correct significant inaccuracies quickly. See Section 2 Impartiality and Live Output guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scepticism with statistics and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics and numbers should not be taken at face value; they must be explained, contextualised, weighed, interpreted, challenged where appropriate, and presented clearly with attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify statistics, explain caveats and limitations, use a range of evidence to contextualise magnitude and importance. See Section 11 on Statistics, Data, Polls and Surveys and Reporting Statistics guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualise reporting of risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporting of risk can affect public perception; content makers should avoid worrying audiences unduly and contextualise reports to be clear about the scale of risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular care in health, crime, economy, weather or climate stories; consider emotional impact of pictures and testimony. See Sections 11 and 8 and Reporting Statistics guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-generated content must be verified and labelled
rubrics_metrics.description: It should not be assumed that user-generated material is accurate; it may need to be verified and it should always be clearly identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether contributors have vested interests; user-generated content may not provide a complete picture. See guidance on User-Generated Contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify material found online
rubrics_metrics.description: Even apparently reliable internet sources may not always be accurate or complete; it may be necessary to check who runs a site or confirm with the individual/organisation that material is genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply internet research guidance; corroborate online material with other sources where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fact from rumour
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact must be distinguished from rumour, particularly on social media where misinformation/disinformation may be deliberate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that error/rumour spreads quickly and corrections get less attention; apply additional scrutiny if using social media items to corroborate facts and attribute material not gathered directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat third-party material with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Material supplied by third parties (including news providers) needs appropriate caution, taking account of the reputation of the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBC should normally only rely on an agency report if it can be substantiated by a BBC journalist or if sourced from a reputable news agency; use third-party material only if credible and reliable; follow BBC credit guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with video and audio news releases and outside-supplied material
rubrics_metrics.description: Content makers should be reluctant to use video/audio news releases or material (voice notes) supplied by outside parties who may have vested interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such material can avoid scrutiny and may be inaccurate; extracts should not normally be used unless the BBC cannot gather it itself and there is editorial justification. Any use must be clearly labelled with who supplied it and relevant circumstances. See Video and Audio News Releases guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and contemporaneous note-taking and records
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate, reliable and, wherever possible, contemporaneous notes of all significant research and relevant information must be taken. Records should be kept of documents, notes, emails, social messages etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records should allow double-checking, particularly at scripting stage; for serious allegations from anonymous sources keep full, timely notes. See Investigations guidance and cross-references to Privacy and Fairness sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not knowingly materially mislead audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC must not knowingly and materially mislead audiences with the content it produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers may need to clarify the nature of some content by labelling (verbally, textually, visually or with audio cues) to avoid being misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due accuracy appropriate to output and audience expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Due accuracy must be adequate and appropriate to the output, taking account of subject, nature of content, likely audience expectation and any BBC-provided information that may influence that expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements may vary within a genre (e.g. factual entertainment vs news vs drama); content producers can use narrative techniques but must remain accurate. See guidance on Recording the Natural World, Fictitious News Bulletins, Reporting and Portrayal of Tribal Peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in dataset methodology and check automated analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When analysing datasets the methodology should normally be available to the audience, including relevant uncertainty or margins of error. Automated analysis should be sense-checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly give sense-checks where outcomes seem unusual; see Section 11 on statistics (11.4.23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid omitting significant details
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting significant details may lead to inaccuracy; audiences should be provided with relevant facts, complete information and context to enable accurate understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure completeness of material and context; consider impact of omissions on audience perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify sources and make credentials clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources of information and significant contributors should normally be identified and their credentials made clear so audiences can judge their status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where anonymity is used, explain the extent and provide as much information as possible without misleading about the source's status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity: clarity, protection and mandatory referral for serious unnamed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever anonymity is agreed, both journalist and source must understand the extent of anonymisation; when quoting an anonymous source, especially one making serious allegations, take steps to protect identity but give the audience whatever information is possible without materially misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop — Mandatory Referral: Any proposal to rely on a single unnamed source making a serious allegation or to grant anonymity to a significant contributor making a serious allegation must be referred to Director Editorial Policy and Standards and Programme Legal Advice, who will consider public interest, source credibility, off-the-record substantiation, whether a response has been sought, legal issues, safety concerns and sensitive personal issues. See Sections on Fairness, Investigations and Privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script anonymous allegations carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting of allegations made by an anonymous source should be scripted to explain the nature of the allegation and that it is being made by an anonymous source and not the BBC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allegations are not independently corroborated, consider whether to inform the audience; be explicit about status and limits of corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live unscripted two-ways not normally used for allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Live unscripted two-ways should not normally be used to report allegations; the editor must decide if they are appropriate when breaking a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When following up stories ensure colleagues understand terms for reporting allegations and do so accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Links should lead to credible third-party sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Links from BBC content to sites operated by others should normally lead to credible sites; where editorially justified, link to external sites significant to a story but assess credibility first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Links and Feeds guidance and cross-references to Impartiality and Independence from Commercial Interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable vs unacceptable production techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Production techniques that augment content in a simple and straightforward way (improving clarity, flow or engagement) are normally acceptable; techniques that materially mislead the audience about reality are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable examples: some cutaway shots, set-up shots, asking contributors to repeat insignificant actions. Unacceptable for news/factual output unless signalled: staging or re-staging significant action; inter-cutting that creates materially misleading impressions. Commentary and editing must never give a materially misleading impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital manipulation and synthetic content must not mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Any digital creation or manipulation (including synthetic content) must not distort meaning of events, alter impact of genuine material or otherwise materially mislead audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that manipulated photos/videos/documents have been used in hoaxes; ensure integrity and clearly label where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of automation and AI: risk, oversight and not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of technologies such as automation or artificial intelligence may lead to inaccuracy (algorithmic bias, hallucinations, plagiarism). The BBC must not knowingly and materially mislead audiences through any use of AI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop — Mandatory Referral: A senior editorial figure must be responsible and accountable for deployment and continuing use of AI and should seek advice from Editorial Policy (which may consult AI Risk Advisory Group) before deployment. Independent production companies should discuss proposed uses of AI in commissioning; a senior editorial compliance figure must be accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-driven products are editorial experiences requiring approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Any product that uses AI to distribute or curate content is considered to be an editorial experience and therefore subject to editorial approval and human oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such products must be treated like other editorial outputs with accountability and oversight mechanisms in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about AI use to audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Any use of AI by the BBC must be transparent and clear to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform audiences appropriately and, where helpful, explain not just that AI was used but how and why. See The Use of Artificial Intelligence guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstructions must be evidence-based and identifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstructions in factual programmes should not over-dramatise or be misleading; they should normally be based on substantial and verifiable evidence and identifiable as reconstructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verbal/visual labelling or audio/visual cues (slow motion, grading) so audience can see where recreation begins and ends; news programmes should not normally stage reconstructions of current events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factually based drama should be evidence-based and explain licence
rubrics_metrics.description: When drama portrays real people/events some elements may be fictional; portrayal should be based on substantial, well-sourced evidence wherever practicable and care taken not to distort known facts (including chronology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivities are greater for living people or recent events; explain drama's factual basis or use of dramatic licence clearly. See Fairness and Privacy sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archive material must not mislead and should be labelled
rubrics_metrics.description: Archive material should not be used in a way that materially misleads about a situation, events or subject; material planned for re-use may be inaccurate or out of date and should be made clear as archive where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure any reuse or reversion is checked for current accuracy and label as archive when needed. See Use of BBC Content After Publication or Broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check content prepared earlier against changing circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Content prepared some time before publication/transmission must be re-checked to ensure it has not been overtaken by events (e.g., death of a contributor, arrest or significant life changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to label, announce, alter or remove material as appropriate given changed circumstances; see Use of BBC Content After Publication or Broadcast guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct serious factual errors promptly and appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious factual errors should be acknowledged and mistakes corrected promptly, clearly and appropriately. Corrections should be scheduled to reach the audience affected and should state what was wrong and put it right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Corrections and Clarifications page can be used for public acknowledgment. Stop — Mandatory Referral: Programme Legal Advice must be consulted if a defamatory inaccuracy may have been published or broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct and acknowledge mistakes in online and on-demand content
rubrics_metrics.description: Where content is permanently available or on demand, serious breaches of editorial standards must be corrected and the error acknowledged in a timely manner; content may be removed in exceptional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where mistakes are unlikely to be serious breaches, publish a correction on that platform visible before replay; make clear what changes made unless editorial/legal reasons prevent disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend online text that alters editorial meaning and note changes
rubrics_metrics.description: In online text content, any mistake that alters the editorial meaning should be corrected. It is important to acknowledge what was wrong, correct the error, and make it clear the article has been amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidance on removal of online content and use amendment notices where appropriate (except where editorial/legal reasons prevent disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify nation directors for significant nation-specific output
rubrics_metrics.description: Any content producers intending to produce output about Northern Ireland or significant projects involving the Republic of Ireland should notify the Director Northern Ireland early; producers creating significant national/regional pieces about England, Scotland or Wales who are not based in that nation should inform the director of that nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop: mandatory referral to the relevant director at an early stage for certain NI/ROI and significant national/regional projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive to different political cultures across UK nations
rubrics_metrics.description: The UK has diverse political cultures in the different nations; when UK audiences are affected differently by a story it should be made clear and producers should be careful about references to governmental and legal structures which may vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take account of regional differences in reporting and consult Reporting the UK guidance where necessary.
